content: Yellow fever is an acute viral disease that remains a significant cause of hemorrhagic illness in many African and South American countries, despite the availability of an effective vaccine. The term yellow refers to the jaundice that can develop in some patients. Historically, yellow fever has caused numerous devastating epidemics. For example, during the 1802 Haitian Revolution, French soldiers were severely affected, with more than half of the army succumbing to the disease. Periodic outbreaks in the Western Hemisphere caused thousands of deaths until research in the early 20th century, involving human volunteers (some of whom died), elucidated the mosquito-borne transmission mechanism and led to the development of a vaccine and other preventive measures. Despite the groundbreaking work of Cuban physician Carlos Finlay, American physician Walter Reed, and others over a century ago, unvaccinated populations in developing nations across Africa, Central America, and South America remain at risk. As of 2001, the World Health Organization (WHO) estimated that yellow fever causes approximately 200,000 illnesses and 30,000 deaths annually in unvaccinated populations. Yellow fever has played a significant role in the history of Africa, the Americas, Europe, and the Caribbean. Scientists believe the disease originated in Africa around 3,000 years ago. In 1937, Max Theiler, working at the Rockefeller Foundation, developed a vaccine that provides immunity for ten years or more, effectively protecting travelers to endemic areas and serving as a means to control the disease. Yellow fever is caused by a single-stranded RNA virus belonging to the genus Flavivirus. Transmission occurs through the bite of an infected mosquito, primarily species of Aedes or Haemagogus. Nonhuman and human primates serve as the primary reservoirs of the virus, with human-to-vector-to-human (anthroponotic) transmission occurring. Humans infected with the yellow fever virus (YFV) exhibit high levels of viremia and can transmit the virus to mosquitoes shortly before the onset of fever and during the first 3–5 days of illness. Theoretically, bloodborne transmission can also occur through transfusions or needlestick injuries due to the high viremia levels. The yellow fever virus is an arthropod-borne virus of the Flaviviridae family. Flaviviruses are single-stranded RNA viruses that replicate in the cytoplasm of infected cells. Seven genotypes of the yellow fever virus have been identified, with two in South America and five in Africa. Yellow fever must be differentiated from other diseases that cause fever, diarrhea, dehydration, and tachycardia, such as Ebola, typhoid fever, malaria, Zika virus, and Lassa fever. Yellow fever is endemic and intermittently epidemic in sub-Saharan Africa and tropical South America. Urban yellow fever occurs periodically in Africa and sporadically in the Americas. In Africa, natural immunity accumulates with age, making infants and children the most vulnerable. In South America, the disease is most common among unimmunized young men exposed to mosquito vectors through work in forested areas. A traveler’s risk of acquiring yellow fever depends on several factors, including vaccination status, travel location, season, duration of exposure, occupational and recreational activities, and the local rate of virus transmission at the time of travel. The initial symptoms of yellow fever typically appear 3–6 days after a mosquito bite. These include sudden onset of fever, chills, severe headache, back pain, generalized body aches, nausea, vomiting, fatigue, and weakness. Most individuals recover after these initial symptoms. However, approximately 15% of patients experience a brief asymptomatic period lasting hours to a day, followed by a more severe form of the disease. Complications can include coma, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), kidney failure, liver failure, and shock. While the prognosis is favorable for most patients, with many being asymptomatic or experiencing mild disease and complete recovery, severe cases can lead to significant morbidity and mortality. Patients with yellow fever may present with fever, muscle pain (notably backache), headache, shivering, loss of appetite, and nausea or vomiting. After 3–4 days, most patients improve, and their symptoms resolve. However, 15% of patients enter a toxic phase within 24 hours, during which fever reappears, jaundice develops, and abdominal pain with vomiting occurs. Bleeding (e.g., hematemesis, melena, petechiae, ecchymoses) and epigastric tenderness, with or without hepatomegaly, may also be observed. Kidney function deteriorates in severe cases. Laboratory findings in yellow fever patients may include leukopenia or leukocytosis, bleeding dyscrasias, thrombocytopenia, and elevated bilirubin and transaminase levels. Diagnosis is typically confirmed by testing serum for virus-specific IgM and neutralizing antibodies. In some cases, the virus can be detected in blood samples collected early in the disease course. There are no approved antiviral treatments for yellow fever, making vaccination a critical preventive measure. Treatment is symptomatic and supportive, focusing on fluid replacement, managing hypotension, and blood product transfusion in severe cases. Dialysis may be required in cases of acute renal failure. Primary prevention of yellow fever involves vaccination and vector control. The yellow fever vaccine is recommended for individuals aged nine months or older who are traveling to or living in areas at risk for yellow fever virus transmission in South America and Africa. Some countries may require proof of vaccination for entry. Preventing mosquito bites is the most effective way to avoid mosquito-borne diseases, including yellow fever.
